title: The other two groups, and asking questions
goal: Complete the present tense by adding the **-er** and **-ir** groups, then set up eight question words that open real conversations.
bekal: conjugate -er and -ir verbs for five subjects
use eight question words without changing the sentence order
answer questions by repeating the verb, like Brazilians do

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Uma entrevista rápida
dialogs.intro: Class assignment: every student interviews their deskmate with ten questions.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Moro perto daqui, na Vila Mariana.
lines.id: I live near here, in Vila Mariana.
lines.literal: I-live near from-here, in-the Vila Mariana.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Com dois amigos. A gente divide um apartamento.
lines.id: With two friends. We share an apartment.
lines.literal: with two friends. we we-divide an apartment.

lines.speaker: Carla:
lines.text: O que você come no café da manhã?
lines.id: What do you eat for breakfast?
lines.literal: what you you-eat in-the coffee of-the morning?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Como pão com queijo e bebo café.
lines.id: I eat bread with cheese and drink coffee.
lines.literal: I-eat bread with cheese and I-drink coffee.

lines.speaker: Carla:
lines.id: Do you drink your coffee black?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Bebo. E você, o que você prefere?
lines.id: I do. And you, what do you prefer?
lines.literal: I-drink. and you, what you you-prefer?

lines.speaker: Carla:
lines.text: Prefiro chá. Por que você aprende português?
lines.id: I prefer tea. Why are you learning Portuguese?
lines.literal: I-prefer tea. for what you you-learn Portuguese?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Because I want to live here.

lines.speaker: Carla:
lines.text: Quando você volta para a Indonésia?
lines.id: When are you going back to Indonesia?
lines.literal: when you you-return for the Indonesia?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Não sei ainda. Talvez em dezembro.
lines.id: I don't know yet. Maybe in December.
lines.literal: not I-know yet. maybe in December.

notes: **Por que and porque — two words one space apart.** *Por que* (two words) means "why" and is used to ask; *porque* (one word) means "because" and is used to answer. They sound exactly the same, so your ears can't tell them apart — only your hand needs to be careful.

**Answering by repeating the verb, once more.** *Você bebe café puro?* → *Bebo.* Notice that what's repeated isn't the form in the question (*bebe*) but the form **for I** (*bebo*). That's what makes this habit double as verb practice.

**Café da manhã is literally "coffee of the morning"**, and it means breakfast — in Brazil, breakfast really is defined by its coffee. *Café puro* means coffee without sugar, and you need to ask because in Brazil coffee comes **already sweet** unless you say otherwise.
**Preferir has a change in its stem**: *eu pref**i**ro*, but *você pref**e**re*. The *e* becomes *i* only for "I". A small group of -ir verbs behaves this way, and they're all gathered in unit 12.
**Talvez** means "maybe" and is used constantly to soften an answer. Together with *não sei ainda* ("I don't know yet"), it's a polite tool for not answering without sounding evasive.

grammars.title: -er and -ir verbs
body: The two remaining groups, and the good news is that their endings are almost the same. Compare all three side by side.
after: **The first row is the same for all three.** The "I" form always ends in **-o**, with no exceptions among regular verbs. A simplification worth being grateful for.
**The -er and -ir groups differ in just one row**: the *nós* form (*comemos* versus *abrimos*). The other four rows are identical. So you're not really learning three systems, but one and a half.

⚠️ Remember how *-em* at the end is said: **ayn**. So *comem* sounds like KOH-mayn and *abrem* like AH-brayn. Compare *-am*, which is said **own** (*falam* = FAH-lown). These two endings sound very different even though both mean "they".

grammars.title: Common -er and -ir verbs
body: All the regular ones are gathered here. The irregular ones are waiting in unit 12.
after: **Estudar and aprender aren't the same.** *Estudar* means sitting down and studying; *aprender* means actually learning it. *Eu estudo português mas não aprendo nada* is a perfectly sensible sentence — and a sad one.

**Assistir also needs a little word**, like *gostar de*: *assistir **a** um filme*. But in everyday Brazil that *a* is dropped without mercy: *Eu assisto filme todo dia*. That spoken form is what you'll hear.

grammars.title: Eight question words
body: They all go at the **start of the sentence**, and the rest of the sentence doesn't change at all. No flipping, no helper verb — unlike English *do you* / *are you*.
after: **The preposition moves to the front together with the question word**: *Com quem você mora?* ("With whom do you live?"), *De onde você é?* ("Where are you from?"), *Para quem é isso?* ("Who is this for?"). English leaves it at the end (*Who do you live with?*); Portuguese never does.

**In conversation, o que is often shortened to just que**: *Que você quer?* And it's often lengthened to *o que é que*: *O que é que você faz?* — both are common, and the second is actually heard more often in Brazil even though it looks more complicated.

⚠️ **Como means "how", and also "what… like" for characteristics.** "What's he like?" is *Como ele é?* But careful: *como* is also "I eat" from *comer*. Context tells them apart, and it's never a real problem.

blocks.text: Portuguese has *sim* and *não*, but Brazilians rarely use them on their own. The usual way is to **repeat the verb** in the right form.

To sound warmer, add *sim* after it: *Falo, sim.* To say no politely, repeat *não* twice: *Não, não falo.* This repeating habit sounds strange at first — a bit like English "I do" / "I don't" — but it's the best grammar practice there is: every answer makes you choose the right form.
Enough for breakfast and a first conversation about tastes. The full menu is waiting in unit 9.

*Arroz e feijão* — rice and black beans — is the pair that shows up on almost every Brazilian table, lunch and dinner. The expression *arroz com feijão* is even used figuratively for "something ordinary but always reliable".
Notice that the first three sentences make you choose the right possessive ending.

items: This is my father → *Esse é o meu pai*
This is my mother → *Essa é a minha mãe*
Our house is big → *A nossa casa é grande*
My father's car → *o carro do meu pai*
Her sister is married → *A irmã dela é casada*
